units.text: On the second of August, 1914, German soldiers crossed the border into Luxembourg.
They came by road and by rail, and they took the capital's railway station and the key bridges within hours.
This was a plain violation of the treaty of 1867, which guaranteed Luxembourg's perpetual neutrality.
Germany said it was only protecting the railways, which were vital to its plan to invade France through Belgium.
Luxembourg's government protested, but it had no army worth the name and no way to resist.
A popular story says that the young Grand Duchess Marie-Adélaïde drove to the Adolphe Bridge and tried to block it with her car.
Whether that is exactly true or not, it captures the helplessness of the moment.
A country that had trusted a piece of paper for fifty years was now occupied.
The occupation was strange. Germany allowed the Luxembourg government to continue operating, and promised not to harm the country.
But the economy was tied into the German war machine, food grew scarce, and many Luxembourgers felt trapped.
Thousands of young men slipped away to join the French army, fighting under the French flag against the occupiers of their homeland.
The Grand Duchess, who was very young, very Catholic, and very conservative, was in an impossible position.
She remained in the country and kept up official contacts with the occupying authorities, including meeting with the German Crown Prince.
When the war ended in November 1918, those meetings came back to haunt her.
The victorious Allies, France and Belgium especially, accused her of being pro-German.
Her reputation collapsed. Crowds demonstrated against her, and the French and the Americans refused to deal with her.
In January 1919, Marie-Adélaïde abdicated in favor of her younger sister, Charlotte, who was twenty-two.
Marie-Adélaïde left the country, entered a convent in Italy, and died in 1924, aged only twenty-nine.
But the monarchy itself was now in question.
In September 1919, Luxembourgers voted in a double referendum.
The first question asked whether they wanted to keep the dynasty, and about seventy-eight percent said yes.
The second question asked what kind of economic union they wanted with a larger neighbor, and about seventy-three percent chose France.
But France turned the offer down, and so Luxembourg turned to Belgium.
In 1921, the two countries formed an economic union, which shared a customs area and tied the Luxembourg franc to the Belgian franc.
That union lasted until both countries adopted the euro.
The year 1919 also brought a political revolution.
A revision of the constitution introduced universal suffrage, which for the first time included women.
In that year's elections, women voted in Luxembourg for the first time, and a woman was elected to parliament.
The next two decades were a time of quiet transformation.
Charlotte, a poised and popular young monarch, married Prince Felix of Bourbon-Parma in 1919.
Their son Jean was born in 1921, and the family became beloved symbols of national unity.
The steel industry prospered, then suffered in the Depression.
And in 1929, Luxembourg passed a law that made it unusually attractive for holding companies, which was the first small step towards the country's future as a financial center.
In 1933, a powerful commercial radio station, Radio Luxembourg, began broadcasting from the country.
It used a strong transmitter, and its programs were in several languages.

It was a business as much as a broadcaster, selling advertising across the borders, and in time it would become one of the most famous radio stations in Europe, bringing popular music into homes across Britain and the continent.
But the shadow of Germany was growing again.
And on the tenth of May, 1940, it fell.
German forces invaded Luxembourg at dawn as part of their attack on France and the Low Countries.
The country was overrun in a single day.
Grand Duchess Charlotte and her government had already decided to leave, and they escaped across the border into France.
From there they went to Portugal, then to London.
Charlotte spent much of the war in exile, in Britain and Canada, and became a voice of the country.
Her radio addresses over the BBC, broadcast to Luxembourg, were heard in secret by people in the occupied country, and they gave courage to many.
What happened next was more brutal than in the First World War.
Hitler's Germany did not treat Luxembourg as a neutral occupied country.
It treated Luxembourg as German.
The man in charge, Gustav Simon, was the Nazi regional governor of the neighboring Koblenz-Trier district, and he was given authority over Luxembourg in the summer of 1940.
His goal was to make the country fully German.
The campaign of Germanization was thorough and petty at once.
The French language was banned.
People were told to change their names, street signs were repainted, and even French words in everyday speech were forbidden, so that a polite merci had to become danke.
Political parties and trade unions were abolished.
Luxembourgers were declared to be Germans of the Moselle region, and sooner or later were expected to join the German war effort.
Then, in October 1941, the Nazi authorities arranged a census.
It had three questions: what is your nationality, what is your mother tongue, and what is your ethnicity?
The Germans expected everyone to answer German, which would prove that Luxembourg was a German land.
But resistance organizers spread the word quietly, and the answer they urged was Luxembourgish, three times.
And so more than nine in ten people wrote Luxembourgish on every line.
The Germans were furious, and they canceled the census.
The Jewish community of Luxembourg, a few thousand people before the war, was persecuted from the first days of the occupation.
Many managed to flee, but more than a thousand were deported to ghettos and camps in the East, and only a small number survived.
The crisis came in the summer of 1942.
On the thirtieth of August, Simon announced that young Luxembourgers would be drafted into the German army.
Within hours, a spontaneous general strike began.
It started in the town of Wiltz, in the north, and spread to the steel towns, to the mines, to schools, to government offices.
Workers walked off their jobs.
Trains stopped. Simon declared a state of emergency, and the Gestapo moved in.
A special court sentenced about twenty strikers to death, and they were shot within days.
The strike was crushed, but it is one of the proudest moments in Luxembourg's national memory, because it was an act of mass defiance in the middle of a brutal occupation.
And the draft went ahead anyway.
Around twelve thousand Luxembourgers were forced to serve in the German army.
About thirty-five hundred of them deserted or went into hiding, and their families were deported to labor camps in Germany and Silesia.
Somewhere between twenty-five hundred and twenty-eight hundred of the conscripts were killed or went missing at the front.
And so the war divided families, and it left a scar that took generations to heal.
Many Luxembourgers fought on the Allied side too.
In Britain, a small Luxembourg unit served in the Allied armies.
And Charlotte's son, Prince Jean, joined the British Army's Irish Guards and took part in the Allied advance after the Normandy landings.
Liberation came in September 1944.
American troops entered Luxembourg City on the tenth, to scenes of wild celebration.
But the country's ordeal was not over.
In December, Hitler launched his last great offensive in the Ardennes forests, the Battle of the Bulge, and the fighting swept straight across northern Luxembourg.
Towns like Wiltz, Clervaux and Vianden were battered, and Wiltz, which had been the cradle of the 1942 strike, was nearly destroyed, earning the title of martyr town.

Meanwhile General Patton's Third Army made its headquarters in Luxembourg City, and from there launched the counterattack that helped save the surrounding region, including the besieged town of Bastogne, just across the border in Belgium.
When the battle ended in January 1945, Luxembourg was free again, but exhausted and scarred.

Patton himself died in December 1945 after a car accident in Germany, and he was buried, at his own wish, among his soldiers, in the American military cemetery at Hamm, just outside the capital, where more than five thousand American servicemen rest today.
In barely a quarter of a century, Luxembourg had been invaded twice by its giant neighbor.
The old strategy of neutrality, of staying quiet and hoping to be left alone, had failed twice, catastrophically.
The country now had to find a new way to survive.
And it did. In the next chapter, we meet the Luxembourgers who decided that the answer was not to hide from Europe, but to help build it.
